sources.parts: Bark sewn over a frame of white cedar ribs, sheathing and gunwales, about half of each by weight
sources.shell: Balance: bark half a centimetre thick, lined all over by the cedar sheathing, 1/8 in thick (native-art-in-canada.com/birchbarkcanoes.html), so a blow splits both. A breaker bends bark and sheathing together between the ribs, by the model every 4 voxels
sources.depthMetres: Keel to gunwale amidships: a 4 cm draft with one paddler in a 30 kg hull and about a quarter metre of side above it
sources.waterplaneSquareMetres: A 4.5 m canoe 0.75 m wide, fine at both ends, so that 600 L aboard settles her by her quarter metre of side

sources.time: A held action lasts the real time of that one piece of work over sixty: game time runs 30 times faster than real time, and boat work is halved again
sources.barkSeconds: Scoring a five-metre sheet along the trunk and around it, then prying and peeling it whole: some 20 to 40 minutes (an estimate; robin-wood.co.uk, 2014, describes the work but gives no time)
sources.trunkBlocks: The sheet is the canoe's whole length, five metres
sources.frame: Fitting one lath, about three minutes: a steamed rib has to be driven in within a couple of minutes, before it cools (robin-wood.co.uk, birch bark canoe build, 2014)
sources.lashing: One rope is ten metres of lashing, some fifty turns, each through a hole made with an awl: about a quarter of an hour (an estimate). The canoe takes as much as her gunwales and stems need, groups of eight to ten turns two inches apart (Adney & Chapelle 1964), counted by her shape's builder
sources.pitch: About a quart of pitch for a canoe (forums.wcha.org, bark pitch questions), one vanilla pot of pitch, a quarter litre to each of her four seams; pitching them all about half an hour (an estimate)
sources.ribs: Ribs bent in wet hold their bend once dry, a couple of days (the Lac du Flambeau build, canoe.csumc.wisc.edu): their laths dry as they would in the bundle
sources.framePart: Her frame is the wood of her laths: its share and the weight it was set for are white cedar's, its strength and density are those of the wood split

sources.bowOnDrag: A fine bow parts the water with next to no pressure drag at a paddler's speeds: her drag ahead is the friction on her wetted surface
sources.broadsideDrag: A hull's side across the flow: a round bottom and its mirror in the surface make a cylinder of her length to twice her draft, which takes about 1.0 (Hoerner 1965, Fluid-Dynamic Drag, ch. 3: 1.2 across a subcritical flow, 0.82 of it for a cylinder ten times as long as it is thick)

sources.heave: A 30 kg bark hull rises with the crest
sources.capsizeBreakerMetres: Seamanship: a breaking wave as high as an open boat's beam can roll it over
sources.rollResponse: Narrow and round in section: quick to roll
sources.pitchResponse: Light and short, it lifts to each swell

sources.capacityLitres: A 5 m hull, about 0.7 m wide and 0.35 m deep inside, half of its box
sources.deckSquareMetres: The open hull, 5 m by 0.7 m, catches the rain
sources.drainLitresPerHour: Pitched seams hold; a holed hull is the integrity's business
